title: Map, mirror, or rite
hookLine: one book about death, three ways a family can hear it
carry: a book about the dead, read to the living
tomorrow: one baby, six mothers. what does he do?
last: A HARD RIVER, AND A WAY ACROSS.

lines: IS SHE REALLY ON A ROAD?
A MAP, A MIRROR, A RITE.
cards: At a funeral, a friend leans over and asks quietly: do you think she's really on a road somewhere?
Three people in the same family could answer three different ways, and all three could be sitting in the room when the Garuda Purana is read. A map, a mirror, or a rite. Here is each one at its best.

teach.h: READ IN THE DAYS OF MOURNING.

teach.b: In many Hindu homes, especially in North India, a priest reads from the Garuda Purana in the days of mourning after a death: Garuda's questions, Vishnu's answers, read aloud while the family sits and listens.
Some families take the passages as a description of what happens: the preta given a body of rice, the road to Yama, the river, the gifts. Its strength is that it takes the text at its word.
The dead have a real future, and what the family does really reaches them. Nothing is only a symbol; every offering counts. Second, the mirror.

teach.h: THE MIRROR: HOW WE TREAT PEOPLE.
teach.b: Some readers hear the road and the hells as pictures of what cruelty does, written so no one forgets that how we treat people matters.
Its strength: it keeps the full moral weight of the passages for someone who can't take the geography literally. The river still warns, and kindness still eases the way. Third, the rite.
Some hear the reading mainly as something done in a house of mourning.

teach.h: THE RITE: WHO'S IN THE CHAIRS.
teach.b: Look at who's in the chairs: an aunt who hasn't slept, kids who don't follow the Sanskrit, a neighbor with food.

The book is about the dead and read to the living. It gives grief a schedule, tasks and days to keep, and it keeps turning to things a listener can still do. That is why the text praises the hearing of it.
Some families hold all three at once. This path won't say which is right. It only points to who's listening.

how: In many Hindu families, especially in North India, a priest reads from the Garuda Purana during the days of mourning after a death; how families understand it, as description, moral teaching or rite, differs from family to family.

o: a Purana of Vishnu's answers about death and more
a funeral song sung only by the eldest son
a list of the dead kept by a family's priest

games.q: three ways to hear it — tap the pairs.

s: the text says only one reading of the road is allowed
families read it as a map, a mirror or a rite, and some hold all three.
the Garuda Purana praises the hearing of it
it treats the reading itself as something that does good.

games.q: your cousin reads the Garuda's road as literally true; you hear it as a moral mirror. what's the strongest case for her view?
o: it's the only respectful way to read a holy book.
it takes the text at its word: the dead have a future, and offerings really reach them.
it frightens people into being good, which is useful.
games.why: the map reading at its best: nothing is only a symbol, and every offering counts. the mirror and the rite have their own strengths.

practice: Many Hindu homes keep a photo of someone who has died, with a garland and a small lamp beside it. If there's a photo nearby of someone you love, living or gone, rest your eyes on it; if not, bring one to mind.
Notice one small detail you usually miss, and breathe with them there. If you pray, say their name to God.

wordCard.voice: The Garuda. A Purana of Vishnu's answers about death, read in the house to the living who are left.
